kit.name: ELEGOO UNO R3 Super Starter Kit

identity.manufacturer: TowerPro (design origin); many ELEGOO-bundled units are third-party clones of the same design rather than boxed TowerPro-branded parts
generic_equivalents: MG90S (metal-gear variant, heavier, not a drop-in mechanical twin)
identity.package: module, plastic-cased gear motor with a 3-wire cable and connector

function.one_sentence_plain_english: A small motor that moves to whatever angle you tell it and holds that position, instead of spinning continuously like a normal motor.
function.what_it_is_used_for: Robot arms, steering for small RC cars, pan/tilt camera mounts, and any project that needs something to swing to a precise position and stay there.
function.how_it_works_briefly: Inside the plastic case is a small DC motor, a set of reduction gears, and a tiny circuit board with a position sensor (a potentiometer). The circuit compares the angle you asked for, which is encoded as a repeating electrical pulse, against the actual position, and drives the motor until the two match.

pinout.name: Ground
pinout.notes: brown wire on the ELEGOO/generic cable; negative supply return

pinout.name: Signal
pinout.notes: orange or yellow wire; pulse width of 500-2400 microseconds sets the target angle

pins.pin_1_identification: On the 3-pin connector, the wire order printed in the handsontec datasheet's connector diagram, reading from the edge, is Ground, +V Power, Signal; the Signal wire is usually the odd color out (orange/yellow) against two darker wires (red and brown/black).

electrical.absolute_max_voltage: 6V DC, per the handsontec SG90 datasheet
electrical.typical_current: not separately listed for no-load operation in the sources fetched
electrical.max_current: under 500 mA working current, per the tinyosshop retailer listing (stall current under load was not found in a source that loaded)
electrical.logic_level: 5V PWM signal, per the datasheet's control-signal diagram

key_specs.stall_torque_at_4_8v: 1.8 kgf*cm (25 oz-in), per the handsontec datasheet
key_specs.operating_speed_at_4_8v: 0.12 sec / 60 degrees, per the handsontec datasheet
key_specs.rotation_range: approximately 180 degrees total (about 90 degrees each direction from center)
key_specs.weight: 9.0 g, per the handsontec datasheet (tinyosshop's page also lists similar dimensions, cross-checked)
key_specs.dimensions_mm: 23.0 (L) x 12.2 (W) x 29.0 (H), per the handsontec datasheet

visual_identification.shape_and_size: small rectangular plastic-cased motor about the size of a matchbox, with a white plastic splined output shaft on top and mounting tabs with rubber grommets on the sides
visual_identification.color_and_markings: blue plastic case with white lettering, typically reading 'TowerPro' and 'SG90' on the side label; ships with a white output horn/arm and small mounting screws
visual_identification.printed_text_to_look_for: 'TowerPro' and 'SG90' printed on the case; the word 'DIGITAL' should NOT appear (this is an analog servo; a similar blue case marked 'SG90 Digital' or 'MG90S' is a different part)
easily_confused_with: SG90 Digital (different internal control electronics despite a nearly identical case)
MG90S (metal-gear version, heavier, visually similar blue case)

example_connections.uno_pin: Digital pin 9, per the handsontec application example

hazards: internal plastic gears can strip if the arm is forced or the servo is stalled against a mechanical obstruction for an extended time
handling_notes: power the servo once and let it center itself before attaching the arm/horn, so the arm's neutral position lines up with the intended range of motion
avoid running many SG90 servos off the Arduino's own 5V pin at once; each one can briefly draw close to 500 mA, which can brown out the board
common_mistakes: swapping the Signal and +V Power wires, which can damage the servo's internal control circuit
forgetting that attaching Servo.h disables PWM output on certain pins (commonly pins 9 and 10) on many Arduino boards while a servo object is attached

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: servo jitters or buzzes while holding one position
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: weak or noisy power supply, or a poor ground connection
symptoms_and_causes.check: measure voltage at the servo's power pins while it is under load; it should stay close to 4.8-6V without sagging

symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: the Signal wire is on the wrong pin, or the code never calls attach() on that pin
symptoms_and_causes.check: confirm the sketch's myservo.attach() call uses the same pin number as the physical Signal wire

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: servo moves the opposite direction from what's expected
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: the horn/arm was attached at the wrong starting position
symptoms_and_causes.check: detach the horn, command the servo to 90 degrees (center), then reattach the horn pointing straight

troubleshooting.how_to_test_with_a_multimeter: With the servo powered and idle, measure DC voltage between the Red and Brown wires; it should read close to the supply voltage (4.8-6V). A basic multimeter cannot usefully read the fast-changing Signal wire's pulse shape; that needs an oscilloscope or logic analyzer.
